I interpret about two hundred technical meetings a year, and the habit I wish engineers had is the cheapest one there is. Say it back. People do not do it, and when I ask why, the answer is always the same: they think it makes them look slow, or as if they had not been listening. It does the opposite. A check-back takes about four seconds. So you said the valves arrive in June, is that right. Four seconds. And the alternative is that two people leave the call with different numbers and neither of them knows it, which surfaces six weeks later in a purchase order. I will tell you something else, which is the part nobody expects. The people who check back most often on the calls I work on are the native speakers. They are not checking because they did not understand the English. They are checking because a number is a number, and because they have been wrong before.

I am the accent that somebody on the call is struggling with, and I would like to say something about that, because people are very careful with me and it does not help. When somebody pretends to understand me, I find out later, usually when something has been ordered or built the wrong way, and then we are both embarrassed and it costs money. Nobody in Finland is offended by being asked to repeat. I ask other people three or four times a week myself, when I am on a call with Brazil or with India, and it has never once been a problem. The one thing I would ask is this. Do not just say pardon, because then I repeat the whole sentence at exactly the same speed and you lose it again. Tell me which part you missed. Say, I got the fourteen weeks but not what came after. Then I know what to repeat, and I know to slow down at the numbers.

A call with fifteen people is not a conversation, it is a queue, and if nobody manages the queue the fastest speakers fill all of it. That is the real problem, and it has very little to do with language. The people with the most useful thing to say are usually the quietest, and by the time they find a gap the topic has moved on. So at the start of a call I now name who is speaking on each topic. Juha on the valves, Cassio on the buildings, and I will come to the rest of you at the end. It sounds bureaucratic and it saves twenty minutes. The other thing I watch is jargon. On an international call, jargon is the fastest way to lose half the room, and the speaker never finds out, because nobody is going to interrupt a senior person to say they did not understand an acronym. If you are the one speaking, say the words out in full the first time. If you are the one listening, ask. Both of those are cheaper than the meeting you will need afterwards.
